Push 22 Blackjack: How This Rule Quietly Restores the House Edge

Published November 14, 2026 · 7 min read · By the OddsLighthouse Editorial Team

Most blackjack variants that market themselves as "player-friendly" trade one upside for a downside buried somewhere in the fine print — a juicier payout on one hand paired with a worse rule somewhere else that quietly claws it back. Push 22 is maybe the cleanest example of that trade in the entire genre of blackjack side variants, because the rule sounds like a gift and functions almost like the opposite.

What the Push 22 rule actually says

In standard blackjack, if the dealer's hand goes over 21, every player still in the hand wins automatically, regardless of what they were holding. Push 22 changes exactly one thing: if the dealer busts with a total of exactly 22, every remaining player hand ties instead of winning. Bust on 23 or higher, and the dealer still loses the normal way. The number 22 specifically is what gets singled out, because it's both the single most common dealer bust total and the one closest to a made hand.

Everything else about the table typically plays like ordinary blackjack — same hit/stand/double/split rules, same dealer hits-or-stands-on-soft-17 convention as whatever base game it's layered onto. The rule shows up under a few different table names depending on the casino and software provider, but the mechanic is identical: one specific dealer bust total gets converted from a loss into a push.

Why this matters more than it sounds like it should: dealers bust on 22 more often than on any other single total, so converting just that one number from a loss into a push removes a disproportionate share of the house's normal bust-related payouts — not a small, incidental slice of them.

Why 22 specifically is the number that gets targeted

Dealer bust totals aren't evenly distributed across 22 through 26. Because a dealer busting is the result of drawing cards toward a target of 21 and going over, totals closer to 21 are substantially more common than totals further away — 22 shows up as a dealer bust far more often than 26 does, since most bust hands tip over by a small margin rather than a large one. Estimates built from standard dealer-draw simulations generally put 22 at somewhere around a quarter to a third of all dealer busts, depending on the exact ruleset (number of decks, soft-17 rule, and so on) being modeled. That's the single largest bust total by a clear margin, which is exactly why it's the one that got chosen for this mechanic instead of, say, 24 or 25.

If a casino instead ran a "Push 25" or "Push 26" variant, the player-facing damage would be far smaller, because those totals happen much less often. Targeting 22 is what makes the rule financially meaningful for the house rather than a cosmetic footnote.

How much house edge this actually adds

Independent of any other rule changes, converting dealer-busts-on-22 from a win into a push typically adds somewhere in the neighborhood of 2 to 2.5 percentage points to the house edge, depending on the number of decks and the dealer's soft-17 rule. On a base six-deck game with a house edge of roughly 0.5% under optimal basic strategy, that single change alone can push the effective edge up into the 2.5–3% range — several times worse than a well-chosen standard blackjack table, and in the same rough neighborhood as games like double-deck blackjack with a bad 6:5 blackjack payout.

Standard 6-deck blackjack, 3:2 payout, basic strategy~0.5%Baseline

Why it still gets marketed as a player perk

Push 22 tables are almost never pitched honestly as "a 2-point tax on every hand." Instead, the marketing usually frames it as a reassurance: "you can never lose to a dealer bust on 22," which is true in the narrowest literal sense and completely misleading about the net effect. A player who doesn't know the baseline bust-win rate has no way to judge whether that reassurance is actually a good deal, because the framing never mentions what it costs on every other hand where the dealer doesn't bust on exactly 22 — nothing changes for those hands, but the table still has to earn back that giveaway somewhere, and it does so simply by existing as a worse-paying table overall relative to a standard one.

This is a pattern worth recognizing across blackjack variants generally: any rule framed purely as a player protection, with no corresponding mention of what the base game gave up to offer it, is worth running through the math before assuming it's a good deal. Free Bet Blackjack and Blackjack Switch both follow a similar shape — see our guides on Free Bet Blackjack and Blackjack Switch for two more examples of the same trade dressed up differently.

A rule that removes one specific losing outcome for the dealer is not the same thing as a rule that helps you. Always ask what the table gave up elsewhere to offer it — in Push 22's case, that's a meaningful chunk of the house's most common bust total.

Should you ever play a Push 22 table?

If a Push 22 table is sitting next to a standard blackjack table with the same minimums, same number of decks, and a 3:2 blackjack payout, there's essentially no scenario where the Push 22 version is the better mathematical choice — you're paying several extra percentage points of edge for a feature that sounds protective but costs more than it gives back. The only time it's worth a second look is if every other table in the room is running a worse combination of rules (6:5 payouts, poor doubling restrictions, or a continuous shuffler cutting into advantage play), in which case it's a comparison of two bad options rather than one good one against a gimmick. Either way, the move is the same: find the actual house edge for every available ruleset before sitting down, rather than trusting how a table's name or marketing describes its own rules.

Frequently asked questions

Does Push 22 change anything about how I should play my own hand?

No. Basic strategy for hitting, standing, doubling, and splitting stays the same as standard blackjack under the same deck count and dealer rules. The only thing Push 22 changes is how one specific dealer bust total gets settled, not how you should play your cards.

Why is 22 the number used instead of a higher bust total like 25?

Dealers bust on 22 far more often than on any higher total, since most dealer busts tip over the 21 line by a small margin rather than a large one. Targeting a less common bust total would barely affect the house edge, which is why 22 is the number almost every version of this rule uses.

Is Push 22 the same thing as a dealer pushing on any bust?

No. Push 22 only converts the specific total of 22 into a push. A dealer bust on 23, 24, 25, or 26 still loses to every remaining player hand exactly like standard blackjack.

Does Push 22 affect blackjack (a natural 21) payouts?

Not directly — a player blackjack still pays according to the table's normal blackjack payout rule (ideally 3:2). Push 22 only changes the outcome when the dealer specifically busts with a total of 22.
